analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal tax credits for buying new or used electric vehicles and installing charging stations.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Ways and Means Committee since its February 2025 referral with no hearing, no markup, and no vote, and its 13 cosponsors are all Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would wipe out four existing federal tax credits: up to $7,500 off a new electric vehicle, up to $4,000 off a used one, up to $40,000 for a business buying a clean commercial vehicle, and up to $1,000 for a person or $100,000 for a business installing an electric-vehicle charging station. It would take effect 30 days after the president signed it. Repeal would raise the effective price of electric cars for buyers while saving the federal government the cost of the credits.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the federal Treasury would keep the money it now spends on the credits, and makers and sellers of gas-powered vehicles would face less-subsidized competition from electric models. Buyers of electric cars would lose the most in dollar terms, especially anyone counting on the $4,000 used-vehicle credit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal taxpayers and conventional auto sellers

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the credit for new clean vehicles, worth up to $7,500 per vehicle through 2033.

It repeals the credit for used clean vehicles (up to $4,000), the commercial clean vehicle credit (up to $40,000), and the tax credit for installing electric-vehicle recharging equipment (up to $1,000 for individuals, $100,000 for businesses).
Repeal would reduce federal spending on these subsidies, since the credits are paid for out of the Treasury.

analysis.who_pays: Anyone buying a new or used electric vehicle would pay up to $7,500 or $4,000 more out of pocket, and electric-vehicle makers, dealers, and charging-station installers would lose the demand the credits support.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would raise the net cost of a new electric vehicle by up to $7,500 and a used one by up to $4,000, making electric cars more expensive relative to gas-powered cars for ordinary buyers.
The used-vehicle credit in particular has supported lower- and moderate-income buyers, and repealing it removes a discount available to households that cannot afford a new electric car.
Repeal would eliminate the tax credit for installing recharging equipment, which businesses and homeowners use to build out charging infrastructure, leaving fewer chargers in place.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the credits are expensive: the commercial vehicle credit alone is worth up to $40,000 per vehicle and often goes to businesses, so the fairest criticism of the credits is not that they should survive untouched but that repeal removes help for individual buyers along with business subsidies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill saves federal money, but it does so by taking a purchase discount away from car buyers rather than by trimming the credits in a targeted way. The business-facing portions (up to $40,000 per commercial vehicle and $100,000 per charging installation) and the consumer-facing portions (up to $7,500 per new car and $4,000 per used car) are repealed together, so a revenue-saving measure also makes electric cars costlier for working families. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much weight you give the budget savings versus cheaper electric transportation.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in February 2025 and has not moved since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jodey Arrington introduced the bill on February 14, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The action history shows no activity after the referral: the bill has not had a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
Thirteen House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats or independents did.

The bill text would strike the new, used, and commercial clean vehicle credits and exclude electric-vehicle recharging property from the refueling-property credit, effective for purchases made more than 30 days after enactment.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has changed position because the bill never advanced: electric-vehicle buyers and the electric-vehicle industry keep the credits the bill would repeal, and taxpayers continue paying for them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: EV buyers and makers, so far

for.name: Rep. Jodey Arrington
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the clean vehicle and charging-station tax credits and referred it to Ways and Means.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a committee markup or floor action since its February 14, 2025 referral; the action history shows nothing after the referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 supporters — the sponsor and 13 cosponsors — are House Republicans, and no Democrat or independent has joined; no vote has occurred to show how the parties would split.

industries.note: Repeal would strip the up-to-$7,500 and up-to-$4,000 purchase credits that currently lower the price of their products, cutting sales. Their loss runs alongside the buyer's loss: both sides of the transaction lose the subsidy.
The bill would exclude recharging property from the refueling-property credit, eliminating up to $1,000 for individuals and $100,000 for businesses that install chargers, slowing charging buildout.

Without the credits, electric cars cost more relative to gas models, shifting buyers toward conventional vehicles. Their relative gain comes from making the cheaper-to-fuel alternative pricier for consumers.
The bill repeals the commercial clean vehicle credit worth up to $40,000 per vehicle, raising the cost of electrifying delivery vans, trucks, and business fleets.

analysis.trajectory: With only 13 of 223 House Republicans backing it and no committee action since February 2025, the bill is unlikely to get a markup or floor vote this Congress. Bills that sit this long in Ways and Means with a small cosponsor list almost always die at the end of the two-year session. The credits it targets could still be repealed or changed through a larger tax bill rather than this one.
